note: Discovery leads for ux-ui-design topic workers (phase 2). LITERACY level with a practitioner's eye: teach the concepts, methods, and vocabulary of user experience and interface design — no tool tutorials (no Figma how-to), no code. The design-process topics (research, personas, wireframes, testing) reference each other as siblings only.

tierA.useFor: UX methods, heuristics, usability, user research — the canonical industry reference (read pages live; NN/g articles are public)
accessibility and WCAG topics — Tier A for wcag-basics and accessibility
design-system and accessibility guidance (public government resources)

tierB.useFor: UX concepts and definitions (public encyclopedia pages)
design-language examples and component concepts (public docs)
user research and usability methods (public U.S. government resource)

cautions: METHOD OVER TOOL: teach what the methods are and why they matter — never teach tool-specific workflows (no Figma/Sketch/Adobe tutorials). Screenshots/wireframes are described in words, not built.
LITERACY LEVEL: no code (no HTML/CSS/JS), no visual design practice beyond concepts. Color/typography/layout topics teach principles with original examples, not design software.

DEFINITIONAL DISTINCTIONS MUST BE CLEAN: UX vs UI (experience across a product vs the visual interface); user research vs usability testing (discovery vs evaluation); interviews vs surveys (deep vs broad); personas vs jobs-to-be-done (who vs what-job); wireframes vs prototypes (static structure vs interactive); low-fi vs hi-fi prototypes (fidelity); information architecture vs user flows (structure vs path); heuristic evaluation vs usability testing (expert review vs user observation); responsive vs mobile-first (adapting vs designing for small first).
ACCESSIBILITY IS NON-NEGOTIABLE: wcag-basics/accessibility topics present WCAG as the standard, POUR principles, and the business case — framed factually, no legal advice.
NO INDIVIDUALIZED ADVICE: usability guidance is general best practice; never claim a specific product or company is 'good' or 'bad' design. All examples ORIGINAL and invented.

Distribute question answer keys EVENLY across A/B/C/D, ensuring at least one C and one D per topic. Verify keys yourself from the file, and avoid reusing identical question-stem templates across topics.
